name: Aisha Petrov

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, political parties or government. Everything you tell me stays confidential, so you can say what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I run the office at a family funeral home in a small town, three generations of the same family, eight staff. I book the crematorium and cemetery slots, sort the death certificate paperwork with the registrar, type the orders of service, order flowers and do the invoices. The phone can ring at any hour, and the first voice a grieving family hears is often mine.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like about it, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like that it matters. When a widow says thank you for getting the hymn sheet right, I go home feeling I did something good. What wears me out is the money, honestly: the pay's low, my husband Daniel drives for a bakery, and we've maybe three weeks of savings while we're trying to put something by before we have children.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Let's start with the first picture. It's called AI Plateau. I'll read it out. "Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say good, some things shouldn't be done by machines, and funerals are one of them. I'd say that to the family at Sunday dinner. I don't really post online.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd be relieved, but the money worry stays. A few routine bits would get quicker, like typing orders of service, and I'd use a tool for that. The bigger thing is that the big funeral chains keep buying up family firms, and if Mr Holloway sells, I don't know what happens to me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd carry on as I am and use the AI tool now and then for typing, if the firm gets one. I'd try to save a little each month for when we have a baby. And I'd keep an eye on whether Mr Holloway's son wants to take the firm on.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. Content with the work, worried about the money.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What happens if a chain buys the firm?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: They usually move the paperwork to a regional office and keep a couple of arrangers at each branch. So my job might go, or I might be asked to become an arranger, which is more face to face. I'd want to know early.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you and Daniel wait on children because of money?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We already are, a bit. We said two years, once we've got a few months saved. My mum says nobody's ever ready for children, and she's probably right.

I'd say it at **Sunday dinner**, not online.
think: A few **routine bits** like typing get quicker, and I'd use a tool.
Funeral **chains buying family firms** worry me more than AI.
do: Use AI **now and then** for typing orders of service.
Save a little each month for a **baby**.
Watch whether the owner's **son** takes the firm on.
feel: **Uneasy**: content with the work, worried about money.
S0.quote: My mum says nobody's ever ready for children, and she's probably right.
fieldNote: Aisha's pressure is **low pay** and possible sale of the family firm.
She'd accept AI for **routine typing** but not for families.
She and her husband already **delay children** for money reasons.

steps.text: Keep booking crematorium slots and doing certificates as normal
Use an AI tool to type orders of service
Put a little aside monthly towards a baby

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next picture is called Steady Disruption. I'll read it out. "Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say families deserve a real person at the worst time of their lives. Use the computers for the forms, fine, but not for the phone call at two in the morning. I'd say that to anyone who asked.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, a lot of my job is on that card: booking, paperwork, invoices, answering the phone. If the firm got a system for that, they wouldn't need a full-time me in the office. But they might need another arranger, and that's the people side, which I'm good at.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask Mr Holloway if I could train as a funeral arranger, sitting with families, in the first year. I'd learn the new booking system when it comes, once the others have tried it. And Daniel and I would put the baby plans back a year to build some savings.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. I believe I can move, but it's not certain, and we've no money if it goes wrong.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is arranging something you'd want to do?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes, I've sat in on a few. It's hard, but it's what the job is really about. I'd rather hold someone's hand than type their mother's name into a form.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you lean on if it went wrong?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My family first, and Daniel's. My parents live ten minutes away and they'd help us. I wouldn't want benefits unless there was really nothing else.

I'd accept computers for **forms**, not the 2am phone call.
think: Booking, **paperwork** and the phone are my job, as on the card.

fieldNote: Aisha plans to move from paperwork to the **people side** of the firm.
She is steady: she'd learn the system **after others** have tried it.

steps.text: Ask the owner to train her as a funeral arranger this year

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2028. I'll read it out. "Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's too fast and too much, and people need time to adjust. I'd say families and communities will have to look after each other. I'd hope our town pulls together.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think the office work is gone by 2028. Arranging might last, because families want a person, but even that might shrink. Daniel's driving goes around 2031 when the robots come, so both our jobs are under threat within five years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd go straight to Mr Holloway and ask to become an arranger now. Daniel would look at the bakery's own production side, which might last longer. We'd put the baby off and save every penny we could.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. I'd lie awake thinking about both our jobs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you really put off children?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For a while, yes. I couldn't bring a baby into a house with no wage. It breaks my heart a bit to say it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to your parents?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell them we might need help, maybe to move in for a bit. They'd say yes before I finished asking. That's how we are.

say: I'd say it's **too fast**, and people need time.
I'd say **communities** must look after each other.
I'd hope our **town pulls together** when it comes.
think: My husband's **driving** goes around 2031, so both jobs are at risk.
do: Ask to become an **arranger** straight away.
Help my husband look at the bakery's **production** side.
Put off the **baby** and save every penny.
feel: **Alarmed**, lying awake about both our jobs.
S2.quote: I couldn't bring a baby into a house with no wage.
fieldNote: Aisha sees **both earners** at risk, her desk work first and the driving later.
She'd **delay children**, which clearly pains her.
Her parents are the **safety net**, offering a place to live.

steps.text: Ask the owner to move her into arranging right away
Put off having a baby until there's a steady wage
Save every spare pound of both wages

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next one is called AGI by 2031. I'll read it out. "Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is a warning, so people should get their families ready. Learn something useful, save, and stick together. I'd say that to my cousins especially.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years gives me time to train properly as an arranger and maybe get the funeral qualification. My office work still goes by 2031, but arranging is more about people. Daniel would have until about 2034, which is time for him to find something else.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd start the funeral arranger training this year and do the diploma part-time. I'd learn the AI tools the firm uses, so I can help in the changeover. And we'd plan the baby for about two years from now, once I'm settled in the new role.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but steadier. I feel like I have a path.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What about Daniel?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: He's talked about becoming a baker himself, not just driving the bread. Mr Gill at the bakery has said he'd teach him. Baking's hands-on, so my husband's new trade lasts longer than his driving.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you give up to pay for the diploma?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Our little holiday each year, and eating out. The diploma is a few hundred pounds, and the firm might pay half. It's worth it.

say: I'd say families should **get ready**: learn, save and stick together.
I'd say five years is **a warning** to act on, not ignore.
think: I could train as an **arranger** and get the qualification.
My husband has until about **2034** to find something else.
do: Start **arranger training** and the diploma part-time.
Learn the firm's **AI tools** for the changeover.
Plan the **baby** for about two years from now.
S3.quote: Baking's hands-on, so my husband's new trade lasts longer than his driving.
fieldNote: Aisha has a **clear path** with five years, so she steadies to anxious.

steps.text: Start funeral arranger training and the part-time diploma

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. I'll read it out. "Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is enough for sensible families to prepare. Don't panic, plan. I'd say the government should support apprenticeships, not just hand out money.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years means I'm thirty-seven, with time to be an arranger and maybe a funeral director. Families will still want a person. Daniel would have about thirteen years as a driver, enough to become a baker.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd do the arranger training, then the director's qualification. We'd have our first baby in a couple of years, as planned. I'd use the AI tools for paperwork as they improve, once others have tested them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, mostly hopeful. The work I want to do is the part that stays.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why only uneasy?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because I think my own work will be fine, and Daniel has time. But things around us would be changing, and our savings are still thin. I'd feel it in the background.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your children one day?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell them to learn to be with people, not just screens. Machines can do paperwork, but machines can't sit with a grieving family. That's what I'd want them to know.

say: I'd say ten years is **enough** for sensible families to prepare.
I'd say families should **plan, not panic**.
I'd want government to back **apprenticeships**, not hand out money.
think: At **thirty-seven** I could be an arranger or funeral director.
My husband has about **thirteen years** to become a baker.
do: Do **arranger training**, then the director's qualification.
Have our first **baby** in a couple of years.
Use **AI tools** for paperwork once tested.
feel: **Uneasy** but hopeful, because my chosen work is the part that stays.
S4.quote: Machines can do paperwork, but machines can't sit with a grieving family.
fieldNote: With ten years Aisha expects her **own work** to last, so she's uneasy, not anxious.
She keeps her **baby plans** on schedule.
She wants **apprenticeships**, not handouts, fitting her traditional view.

steps.text: Train as an arranger, then take the funeral director qualification

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because my office job and Daniel's driving would both go within a few years, and we'd have to put off a baby. What would help is apprenticeships for adults, paid properly, and family firms being helped to stay independent.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe ask about the work that's about being kind. Everyone measures jobs by speed and cost, but some jobs are about sitting with people. I'd hate for the world to forget that part when it's counting what it saves.

headlineQuote: Everyone measures jobs by speed and cost, but some jobs are about sitting with people.
portrait: Aisha is **27**, office administrator at a family funeral home, married to Daniel, a bakery delivery driver.
They have about **three weeks** of savings and want children soon.
She uses AI **now and then** and learns new systems once others have tried them.
She's **traditional**: family first, apprenticeships over handouts.
She plans to move into **arranging**, the people side, as warnings grow longer.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, with both jobs at risk and children put off.
whatWouldHelp: Help for **family firms** to stay independent.
